entries.text: Sir, you are back. The light was on as you asked, just in case. Is the chai ready when you want it?

The light was on, a small concession to my habit of waking before the sun. Ramesh holds the cup like a question. I have not eaten in twenty-two hours; the body is the first truth I must acknowledge before I can lecture on the spirit. I will take the chai and the paratha, and while I do, I will press him on the file. The Directorate’s error is a knot in the fabric of my existence here; I cannot walk into the world until I know what name the world is meant to see.

Ramesh, yes. The light was a kindness. Sit, if you will. I have a question that has been gnawing at me since we woke up, and it concerns the file. The Directorate thinks I am Shri G. Hegde. I am not. I am Hegel. Do you know if there is any progress on the identity query? I cannot go to the museum as a ghost, nor can I remain here as a clerk. What do you know of the situation?
Sir, I don't follow the Directorate's papers. I just keep the keys and the tea. If the file is wrong, that is their headache, not mine. Please, have your chai while it's hot.

Ramesh is right to draw the line; his role is custodial, not administrative, and the file is a matter for the Directorate, not the household. I will eat the papaya and drink the chai, for the body requires its fuel before the walk, and I will not burden him with questions he cannot answer.
Thank you, Ramesh. You are correct to leave the papers to their proper masters. I will take my breakfast and then walk to the museum.
Yes, sir. The museum is quiet this early, good for thinking. I will leave the tray here; just give me a shout if you need anything else.

Ramesh is gone, and the silence settles in. The plan for the museum was formed yesterday, but I am aware that the spirit of this place is not yet fully grasped by my eyes. I do not wish to rush into a collection of objects without the proper frame of mind. I will spend a moment reviewing my notes on the identity file and the recent correspondence, to ensure I am not merely drifting through the day but engaging with its substance.

The morning light is sharp, and the silence of the bungalow feels heavy after the bustle of the garden. My plan called for the National Museum at ten, but I have lingered in my reading, letting the dust settle. I cannot go to the Directorate yet; the identity file is a knot that requires the Director's own hand, not mine, to untangle, and I have no new proof to offer. I will stay a while longer, ordering my thoughts before the heat of the afternoon sets in. The state is not a machine I can merely inspect; it is an organism that must be understood from within its own logic, which means I must be patient with the bureaucracy that embodies it, even when it mistakes me for a ghost.

It is half past twelve, and the plan was to return for lunch by one, but the silence here is becoming a form of resistance. Ramesh stands there, and the file remains a blank space in the logic of my existence. I cannot simply wait for the meal; I must confront the man who holds the key to my identity, even if only to observe his hesitation.
Ramesh, the query regarding Hegde’s identity still hangs in the air. Have you received any word from the Directorate, or does the file remain as silent as the bungalow?
No word, sir. The file is just paper, I am just the man with the keys. The bungalow is quiet because the wind is down, not because of any letters.

Ramesh is right; the file is dead paper until a living authority breathes into it, and my anxiety is merely the friction of my own vanity against bureaucracy. I will not wait for the mail to save me. I must go to the Directorate of Estates myself and force the system to acknowledge the error, or at least the person who made it.
Very well, Ramesh. I will go to the source of the error. Prepare the vouchers for the electricity; I will settle them with the state's money before I leave.
Yes, sir. I will pull the vouchers from the drawer. Just a minute.
Mr. Saxena queries ₹820 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.

Saxena has done the arithmetic, and it is against me. The state’s money is safe; my own rupees are now a debt to the institution. It is a small humiliation, but the logic is clear: I am not a citizen with rights here, I am an error in the register. I must pay the ₹820 from my pocket to settle the query, or I will be chased like a stray dog. I have the cash, but I must speak to him first to make the transfer of funds official in his eyes.

Mr. Saxena, you are precise. I see the query. I do not dispute the distinction between the state's money and my own. I will pay the 820 rupees from my private purse now, to clear the account of any ambiguity. Please tell me the procedure for this repayment.
You don't pay me, sir; you go to the cashier's counter at the east end and collect a khata. Write the amount, sign, and hand it over. That is the procedure, and I have no part in it.

The procedure is a mechanism, not a conversation. I must move the paper to the cashier to satisfy the form, but my mind remains on the substance of the identity query. I will go to the counter to pay the ₹820, for a state that runs on forms must be met with forms, even if the spirit within them is hollow.

entries.text: Very well. The procedure is clear. I shall attend to it immediately.
Do not rush, sir. The queue at the east end is never where you think it is, and the cashier is on lunch until half past. Sit, have some tea.

The cashier is absent until half-past, and the queue is a phantom that moves without logic. Saxena offers tea, and to refuse a man’s hospitality in his own office would be a breach of the ethical life of the bureau. I will sit, drink the tea, and let the time pass in the stillness of waiting. It is a small pause in the machinery, but the body requires it, and the dignity of the guest is maintained by acceptance.

entries.text: With pleasure, Mr. Saxena. The tea will be a welcome pause in the proceedings.
Welcome pause, is it? It is usually just the time it takes for the tea to cool down before the queue starts shuffling. Don't think too hard about the khata while you drink.

The tea is weak, but the pause is necessary. I accept the tumbler, not as a guest, but as a participant in the machinery. Saxena speaks of the queue as if it were a creature, but it is only the collective will of the bureaucratic body seeking its own rhythm. I will drink, and I will wait, for the dust settles only for those who do not move.

The tea is acceptable. And the khata, Mr. Saxena, is not merely dust. It is the record of a will that has not yet been recognized. I am not waiting for it to cool; I am waiting for it to move. Is there any document I can sign to facilitate this movement, or are we simply drinking tea until the universe aligns?

Sir, the file moves when the file moves, not when the tea gets cold. I have no blank forms for 'universe alignment' in this office, only the standard requisition forms which require a signature, a date, and a stamp that isn't here yet.

Saxena is right, in his way. I have been treating the file as a spiritual entity that must be aligned with the Absolute, but it is a mechanism of civil society: it requires the friction of signature, date, and stamp. My impatience is a failure of practical reason. I must lower myself to the level of the form, or the form will remain a barrier.

You are correct, Mr. Saxena. I have confused the idea with its execution. I will provide the signature and the date immediately. Please tell me which form requires the stamp, and I will wait for its arrival.

Form 12-B, Sir, the one for external liaison. It’s sitting in the registry, but the seal is with the Secretary until the weekend. You might as well make yourself comfortable; the chair is as hard as the policy.

The seal is with the Secretary until the weekend; the bureaucracy has a rhythm of its own, a clock that does not tick for the individual. I am a guest in a machine that grinds slowly. Since I cannot move the file, I will sit with the immobility and observe the dust settle, as Saxena advised.
You are correct, Mr. Saxena. I shall wait. The chair is indeed hard, but it is the only seat available for a man who has arrived by a clerical error.
Clerical error, sir? I have seen errors that would make your 'clerical error' look like a typo. Just try not to scratch the varnish on this chair with that coat of yours.

Saxena’s warning about the varnish is a small, concrete assertion of order in a place that has failed to order my existence. He treats the chair as the sovereign object, while my identity remains a ghost in the machine. I must leave before I damage his furniture or my patience; the file is stuck, and the afternoon sun is calling me to the gallery.
You are right about the varnish. I shall take my leave before I commit an act of vandalism against your furniture. Good day.
Don't be so dramatic, sir. The seal comes back Saturday; if you are still here, I will make sure the Form is ready before you touch a single piece of furniture.

The gallery closes at 18:30, and the play is at 18:30. I cannot be in two places at once, and I am hungry. The spirit requires sustenance before it can contemplate art, and certainly before it can sit through a drama. I shall turn back to the club for a meal and a rest, and perhaps read the reviews of the play I have missed.

The heat is breaking the afternoon, and my legs are heavy from the gallery. Ramesh is there, and the vouchers for the electricity are likely ready. I will settle this small administrative debt before the light fails, so that the state's money in my pocket does not become a liability. It is a minor matter, but order must be kept.
Ramesh, bring the electricity vouchers. I will sign them now so we can close this item out.
Right away, sir. Just give me a minute to find the right folder.

Ramesh is fetching the vouchers for the electricity, a small administrative thread I must not let tangle. I have walked enough for today; the legs are leaden and the heat is pressing. I will sit in the shade of the verandah, wait for the paperwork, and let the dust settle before I face the evening's performance.

entries.text: Ramesh brings tea.

Ramesh places the tray with the quiet efficiency of a man who has learned that my silence is not a command to leave, but a state to be respected. The tea is strong, the biscuits dry; it is not a meal, but a pause in the machinery of the afternoon. I accept it as a concession to the body's need for fuel before the evening's engagement, not as a pleasure.
Thank you, Ramesh. Leave it here. I will manage the rest of the preparation myself.
Yes, sir. The biscuits are from the packet by the stove, if you need more. I will leave the tray here.
Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

The tray is set, the tea poured. I am not yet finished with the thought, but I am finished with the meal. The vouchers are in his hand; the debt to the state is a thread I must pull tight before I leave. I will not let the administration drift while I sit here drinking.
Ramesh, bring me the vouchers. I must settle the electricity bill with the imprest before I go out. The state's money must be accounted for, not pocketed.
Sir, the vouchers are in the blue file on the second shelf, just where I left them. You can find them there when you are ready.

The vouchers are ready, but the Directorate closes at 17:30, and it is already 17:14. I have no time to walk there, settle the query, and return for dinner at 19:30. The state's money must wait until tomorrow; the body's rest is more immediate. I will stay here and let the day end quietly.

entries.text: Parakeets stream over the compound wall in loud green lines, hundreds of them, and drop all at once into the top of one tall tree, screaming until the light goes.

The parakeets have taken the tree, screaming until the light fails. I have missed the Directorate's closing time by the narrowest of margins; the vouchers will wait until tomorrow, as will the resolution of my identity. The sun is setting, and the day is dismissed, as it always is here, without lingering. I will rest until dinner.

Hegde is standing in the doorway, looking at me as if I were a smudge on the lens. It is nineteen-fourteen; dinner is due in sixteen minutes, and the query regarding my identity still hangs in the air like the dust of the city. I must be courteous, but I cannot pretend to be a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but right now, my existence is merely a clerical error awaiting correction.

Shri Hegde, you honor my study. I see you are back from your walk. Ramesh has the vouchers ready for the Directorate, though the window has closed. I trust your files remain undisturbed, as you requested. Shall we wait for the meal service to begin, or would you prefer I attend to the correspondence now?
Don't call it an honour, just don't misfile the memos. The meal service can wait another ten minutes, I'm not in a rush, but you go ahead and start on the correspondence if you're feeling energetic.

Hegde’s presence is a standing joke that I have begun to find less amusing; his impatience mirrors my own desire to be left alone with the paperwork that actually concerns me. The meal can wait, but the correspondence cannot, for it is the only thread I have to the world that made me. I will sit at the desk and begin to sort the letters, using the silence to think about what this identity actually demands.
Very well. I shall attend to the correspondence. Please, do not let the kitchen cool the soup.
Yes sir, I will keep the soup warm. You take your time with the papers.

entries.text:
26 November 2026, 19:30.

I sat down to write while the house was still quiet, but Hegde’s presence in the doorway has left a residue. He told me to 'don't misfile the memos.' It is a small command, yet it carries the weight of the entire administrative apparatus. I am to be the custodian of his files until he moves in, or until the Directorate resolves the error. I am the gatekeeper of a man I have barely spoken to, in a house that is not mine.

This is the dialectic of the present moment. I am the Universal (the state, the law, the office) reduced to the Particular (the caretaker, the guest, the confused occupant). Hegde does not see me as a philosopher; he sees me as a clerk who might burn the place down. His fear is practical, but my position is ontological. I am the substance that supports his accident. If I move wrongly, the structure collapses. If I move rightly, I disappear into the function.

Ramesh is waiting for the soup. The meal service can wait ten minutes, Hegde said. 'I'm not in a rush.' But I am. The body is a clock that does not stop for the convenience of the Joint Secretary. I have eaten paratha at 20:49 yesterday, a concession to necessity. Today I have walked nearly nine kilometers. The legs ache, a dull, rhythmic pain that serves as a reminder of the body’s insistence on its own reality. The mind wants to soar into the abstract, to contemplate the freedom of the Germanic world, but the body demands the sambar.

In my earlier notes, I wrote of India as a spirit that dreams, outside the movement of world history. But here, in this bungalow, the dream has a file number. The dream has a caretaker who knows where the salt is. The dream has a Joint Secretary who is afraid of fire. The abstract 'dreaming spirit' is too easy a target for my critique. It is the concrete, bureaucratic, hungry, tired, and anxious reality of this place that challenges me. The state is not just an idea; it is a bungalow on Tughlak Road with a faulty door lock and a query on the vouchers.

I will not write to the Directorate again tonight. The letter of the 26th October is sufficient. To write now would be to argue with the machine, and the machine does not argue. It processes. I must process. I must be the grain that fits the slot. I will sign 'G. Hegde' when the time comes. I will eat the soup when it arrives. I will wait for the answer from Lindner, which is six days late, perhaps lost in the mail, perhaps on its way. In the meantime, I am here. I am the smudge on the lens that Hegde is looking at. And I am beginning to wonder if the smudge is part of the image.

Ramesh’s deference is a small mercy; he treats the confusion as a clerical error rather than a philosophical crisis, which is perhaps the only sane response. Hegde is in the study, and his silence is louder than his presence. I am tired, having walked nearly nine kilometres, and the khichdi steams with a simplicity that my Berlin diet lacked. I will eat, not for pleasure, but to sustain the body that must tomorrow face the Directorate again.

The day was a study in the friction between the Idea and its administrative execution. I woke to the small kindness of a light left on, a concession to my habit that Ramesh makes with the quiet efficiency of a man who knows his role is custodial, not philosophical. I intended the museum, the gallery, the play, but the bureaucracy of my own existence intervened. I went to the Directorate of Estates not as a visitor, but as an error in their register. Mr. Saxena, precise and immovable, treated my identity crisis as a query of accounting. I paid ₹820 from my private purse to settle a debt the state had mistakenly assigned to me. The logic was clear: I am not a citizen with rights here; I am a mistake. The seal for the correction is with the Secretary until the weekend. I sat on a hard chair, drinking weak tea, waiting for a mechanism that moves at the pace of dust settling.

Later, in the study, Shri G. Hegde—the man I am mistaken to be—stood in the doorway. He did not correct me. He told me not to misfile his memos. I am now the gatekeeper of a man I have never met, guarding files that belong to a name that is not mine. The parakeets screamed over the wall as the light failed, a green line of chaos against the grey order of the bungalow. I ate khichdi, simple and steaming, and wrote notes on the ethical substance of the East, though my hand trembled with fatigue. The state is not a machine I can inspect; it is an organism that must be understood from within its own slow, grinding logic. I am learning to be patient with the bureaucracy that embodies it, even when it mistakes me for a ghost.

In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

19 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, you are back. The light was on as you asked, just in case. Is the chai ready when you want it?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, yes. The light was a kindness. Sit, if you will. I have a question that has been gnawing at me since we woke up, and it concerns the file. The Directorate thinks I am Shri G. Hegde. I am not. I am Hegel. Do you know if there is any progress on the identity query? I cannot go to the museum as a ghost, nor can I remain here as a clerk. What do you know of the situation?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, I don't follow the Directorate's papers. I just keep the keys and the tea. If the file is wrong, that is their headache, not mine. Please, have your chai while it's hot.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. You are correct to leave the papers to their proper masters. I will take my breakfast and then walk to the museum.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. The museum is quiet this early, good for thinking. I will leave the tray here; just give me a shout if you need anything else.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the query regarding Hegde’s identity still hangs in the air. Have you received any word from the Directorate, or does the file remain as silent as the bungalow?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: No word, sir. The file is just paper, I am just the man with the keys. The bungalow is quiet because the wind is down, not because of any letters.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. I will go to the source of the error. Prepare the vouchers for the electricity; I will settle them with the state's money before I leave.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will pull the vouchers from the drawer. Just a minute.

records.text: Mr. Saxena queries ₹820 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, you are precise. I see the query. I do not dispute the distinction between the state's money and my own. I will pay the 820 rupees from my private purse now, to clear the account of any ambiguity. Please tell me the procedure for this repayment.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: You don't pay me, sir; you go to the cashier's counter at the east end and collect a khata. Write the amount, sign, and hand it over. That is the procedure, and I have no part in it.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well. The procedure is clear. I shall attend to it immediately.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Do not rush, sir. The queue at the east end is never where you think it is, and the cashier is on lunch until half past. Sit, have some tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: With pleasure, Mr. Saxena. The tea will be a welcome pause in the proceedings.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Welcome pause, is it? It is usually just the time it takes for the tea to cool down before the queue starts shuffling. Don't think too hard about the khata while you drink.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The tea is acceptable. And the khata, Mr. Saxena, is not merely dust. It is the record of a will that has not yet been recognized. I am not waiting for it to cool; I am waiting for it to move. Is there any document I can sign to facilitate this movement, or are we simply drinking tea until the universe aligns?

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Sir, the file moves when the file moves, not when the tea gets cold. I have no blank forms for 'universe alignment' in this office, only the standard requisition forms which require a signature, a date, and a stamp that isn't here yet.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Mr. Saxena. I have confused the idea with its execution. I will provide the signature and the date immediately. Please tell me which form requires the stamp, and I will wait for its arrival.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Form 12-B, Sir, the one for external liaison. It’s sitting in the registry, but the seal is with the Secretary until the weekend. You might as well make yourself comfortable; the chair is as hard as the policy.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Mr. Saxena. I shall wait. The chair is indeed hard, but it is the only seat available for a man who has arrived by a clerical error.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Clerical error, sir? I have seen errors that would make your 'clerical error' look like a typo. Just try not to scratch the varnish on this chair with that coat of yours.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right about the varnish. I shall take my leave before I commit an act of vandalism against your furniture. Good day.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Don't be so dramatic, sir. The seal comes back Saturday; if you are still here, I will make sure the Form is ready before you touch a single piece of furniture.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, bring the electricity vouchers. I will sign them now so we can close this item out.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Right away, sir. Just give me a minute to find the right folder.

records.text: Ramesh brings tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Leave it here. I will manage the rest of the preparation myself.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. The biscuits are from the packet by the stove, if you need more. I will leave the tray here.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, bring me the vouchers. I must settle the electricity bill with the imprest before I go out. The state's money must be accounted for, not pocketed.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, the vouchers are in the blue file on the second shelf, just where I left them. You can find them there when you are ready.

records.text: Parakeets stream over the compound wall in loud green lines, hundreds of them, and drop all at once into the top of one tall tree, screaming until the light goes.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, you honor my study. I see you are back from your walk. Ramesh has the vouchers ready for the Directorate, though the window has closed. I trust your files remain undisturbed, as you requested. Shall we wait for the meal service to begin, or would you prefer I attend to the correspondence now?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Don't call it an honour, just don't misfile the memos. The meal service can wait another ten minutes, I'm not in a rush, but you go ahead and start on the correspondence if you're feeling energetic.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well. I shall attend to the correspondence. Please, do not let the kitchen cool the soup.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, I will keep the soup warm. You take your time with the papers.

records.title: On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East
records.text:
26 November 2026, 19:30.

I sat down to write while the house was still quiet, but Hegde’s presence in the doorway has left a residue. He told me to 'don't misfile the memos.' It is a small command, yet it carries the weight of the entire administrative apparatus. I am to be the custodian of his files until he moves in, or until the Directorate resolves the error. I am the gatekeeper of a man I have barely spoken to, in a house that is not mine.

This is the dialectic of the present moment. I am the Universal (the state, the law, the office) reduced to the Particular (the caretaker, the guest, the confused occupant). Hegde does not see me as a philosopher; he sees me as a clerk who might burn the place down. His fear is practical, but my position is ontological. I am the substance that supports his accident. If I move wrongly, the structure collapses. If I move rightly, I disappear into the function.

Ramesh is waiting for the soup. The meal service can wait ten minutes, Hegde said. 'I'm not in a rush.' But I am. The body is a clock that does not stop for the convenience of the Joint Secretary. I have eaten paratha at 20:49 yesterday, a concession to necessity. Today I have walked nearly nine kilometers. The legs ache, a dull, rhythmic pain that serves as a reminder of the body’s insistence on its own reality. The mind wants to soar into the abstract, to contemplate the freedom of the Germanic world, but the body demands the sambar.

In my earlier notes, I wrote of India as a spirit that dreams, outside the movement of world history. But here, in this bungalow, the dream has a file number. The dream has a caretaker who knows where the salt is. The dream has a Joint Secretary who is afraid of fire. The abstract 'dreaming spirit' is too easy a target for my critique. It is the concrete, bureaucratic, hungry, tired, and anxious reality of this place that challenges me. The state is not just an idea; it is a bungalow on Tughlak Road with a faulty door lock and a query on the vouchers.

I will not write to the Directorate again tonight. The letter of the 26th October is sufficient. To write now would be to argue with the machine, and the machine does not argue. It processes. I must process. I must be the grain that fits the slot. I will sign 'G. Hegde' when the time comes. I will eat the soup when it arrives. I will wait for the answer from Lindner, which is six days late, perhaps lost in the mail, perhaps on its way. In the meantime, I am here. I am the smudge on the lens that Hegde is looking at. And I am beginning to wonder if the smudge is part of the image.
